blocks.text: Structured Data introduced the general idea of rows and columns, and Unstructured Data covered the far more common, free form alternative. Tabular data is a more specific, genuinely practical term, it is structured data arranged in the exact shape a machine learning model actually trains on, with a clear split between the columns used to predict something and the column being predicted.

This topic covers what makes data specifically tabular rather than just generally structured, the feature and target split that every supervised learning problem depends on, the data types that typically live inside a tabular dataset, and the tools genuinely used to work with this shape of data day to day.
1. What Makes Data Specifically Tabular

blocks.alt: Rows and columns together make tabular data

blocks.text: Tabular data is structured data organized specifically for machine learning, where the columns are genuinely split into two roles, feature columns that describe each observation, and typically one target column that holds the value a model is actually trying to predict. A dataset of house sales with square footage, bedrooms, and location as features, and price as the target, is a classic, genuinely tabular dataset.

This distinction matters because not all structured data is immediately tabular in this sense, a database table might mix identifiers, timestamps, and business fields with no clear feature and target split at all. Turning a general structured table into a genuinely tabular, model ready dataset usually means deliberately choosing which columns are features and which single column is the target.
2. The Feature and Target Split

blocks.alt: A table splits into feature columns and a target column

blocks.text: In supervised learning, covered broadly in the introductory module of this course, a tabular dataset is genuinely split into two pieces before training begins. The feature columns, conventionally called X, hold everything the model is allowed to look at, square footage, bedrooms, location. The target column, conventionally called y, holds the one thing the model is actually trying to learn to predict, the price.

This X and y naming convention is genuinely universal across machine learning code and libraries, and it is worth internalizing early, because every regression and classification algorithm covered later in this course expects data handed to it in exactly this split shape, not as one undivided table.

blocks.text: 3. Data Types Genuinely Found Inside a Tabular Dataset

blocks.alt: Tabular data holds numeric, categorical, and date and time columns

blocks.text: A tabular dataset genuinely mixes several different kinds of columns, and telling them apart matters for nearly everything that happens later in this course, especially the Encoding Techniques and Feature Scaling modules. Numeric columns, age, price, temperature, hold genuine numbers a model can compute directly with. Categorical columns, city, color, product category, hold labels with no inherent order between them.

Ordinal columns are a genuinely distinct middle case, a rating of low, medium, or high is categorical looking but has a real, meaningful order between its values. Binary columns, yes or no, true or false, are a simple special case of categorical data with exactly two possible values, common enough that they are usually worth naming separately.

items: Numeric: genuine numbers such as age, price, or temperature.
Categorical: labels with no inherent order, such as city or color.
Ordinal: labels with a genuine, meaningful order, such as low, medium, high.
Binary: exactly two possible values, such as yes or no, true or false.

blocks.title: Why this distinction matters early
blocks.content: Many algorithms genuinely cannot consume categorical or ordinal columns directly, they need to be converted into numbers first, exactly the work covered later in the Encoding Techniques module of this course. Spotting the type of every column early saves real rework later.

blocks.text: 4. What a Row Genuinely Means in Tabular Data

A single row in a tabular dataset is genuinely called an instance, a sample, or an observation, three different words used somewhat interchangeably across machine learning material, all meaning the exact same thing, one complete, individual data point. Every column value in that row genuinely describes that one same instance, never a different one.

This vocabulary genuinely matters because it shows up constantly once this course reaches actual algorithms, a model is trained on a set of samples, evaluated on held out samples, and eventually used to predict on brand new, unseen samples, all built directly on this same row level idea introduced here.
5. The Feature Matrix Shape

blocks.alt: N rows and M columns together form the feature matrix

blocks.text: Once the feature columns are pulled out as X, they genuinely form a matrix, a two dimensional grid of numbers, with a shape typically described as n_samples by n_features, n rows, one per instance, and m columns, one per feature. This shape shows up constantly in error messages and documentation across virtually every machine learning library.

Getting this shape right is genuinely one of the first practical hurdles in any real project, a model trained on a matrix of one shape will genuinely refuse to predict on a matrix of a different shape, which is exactly why the Train Validation Test Split topic next in this module spends real time on keeping this shape consistent across every split of the data.
6. A Worked Example
A small tabular dataset of house sales makes the feature and target split genuinely concrete, using pandas, the standard Python tool for this exact shape of data.

code.content:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({
    "square_feet": [1200, 1800, 950, 2100],
    "bedrooms": [2, 3, 1, 4],
    "location": ["suburb", "city", "suburb", "city"],
    "price": [250000, 400000, 180000, 500000],
})

X = df[["square_feet", "bedrooms", "location"]]
y = df["price"]

print(X.shape)
print(y.shape)

blocks.text: This is genuinely the exact split every regression algorithm covered later in this course expects to receive, X holding the features a model is allowed to see, y holding the single target value it is trying to learn to predict.
7. From Raw Table to Model Ready Data

blocks.alt: A raw table gets cleaned, then encoded and scaled

blocks.text: A raw tabular dataset pulled straight from a source is genuinely rarely ready to train on immediately. It typically needs cleaning, handling missing values and obvious errors, a concern covered in real depth in the Data Quality topic in this module, and then feature engineering, deriving new, more useful columns, covered across the entire Feature Engineering module that follows this one.

Only after both steps does a tabular dataset genuinely become model ready, fully numeric, with a clean X and y split, and no remaining missing values. This progression, raw, cleaned, feature engineered, model ready, is genuinely the backbone of nearly every real machine learning project this course eventually builds toward.

blocks.title: A common early mistake
blocks.content: Trying to train a model directly on raw, uncleaned tabular data genuinely fails or silently produces a poor model. The cleaning and feature engineering stages are not optional extras, they are typically where most of the real work in a machine learning project actually happens.

blocks.text: 8. Tools Genuinely Used for Tabular Data

blocks.alt: Pandas and SQL are the common tools for tabular data

blocks.text: pandas is genuinely the standard Python tool for tabular data, its core DataFrame object is built specifically around this row and column shape, with built in support for exactly the cleaning and feature engineering steps described above. NumPy sits underneath pandas, providing the genuinely fast numeric arrays that the actual computation runs on.

For tabular data that genuinely lives inside a relational database rather than a file, SQL, covered in full depth in the DBMS course on this platform, is typically the tool used to pull the relevant rows and columns out before pandas takes over for the machine learning specific steps.
9. Tabular Data Versus What Comes Next

blocks.alt: Tabular data is covered here, time series data comes next

blocks.text: Everything covered so far in this topic assumes the order of rows genuinely does not matter, shuffle a tabular dataset of house sales and it remains an equally valid dataset. That assumption genuinely breaks the moment time enters the picture, which is exactly the subject of the next topic.

Time Series Data covers the case where row order is not just meaningful but genuinely essential, where yesterday value directly affects today prediction, a fundamentally different situation from the tabular data covered here, and one that changes how splitting, feature engineering, and even basic analysis has to be done.

items: Tabular data is structured data specifically arranged with feature columns and a target column for a model to train on.
The feature and target split, X and y, is a universal convention every supervised learning algorithm expects.
A tabular dataset typically mixes numeric, categorical, ordinal, and binary columns.
A row is called an instance, sample, or observation; the feature matrix has shape n_samples by n_features.
Raw tabular data genuinely needs cleaning and feature engineering before it becomes model ready.
The next topic, Time Series Data, covers the case where row order and time genuinely matter, unlike here.
